evidence.label: Ambiently homeomorphic isolated hypersurfaces of multiplicities two and three
Ambiently homeomorphic isolated hypersurface germs in ℂ⁴ with multiplicities four and five

headline: Two hypersurface germs with the same embedded topology but different multiplicities, against Zariski’s 1971 question.
scope: Isolated hypersurface singularities: multiplicities 2 and 3 in a dimension divisible by eight; 4 and 5 in four variables.
plain: The multiplicity of a singular point is the lowest degree of the equation there. In 1971, Zariski asked whether the shape’s topology near the point always determines that number. The first paper claims two equations with multiplicities two and three whose zero sets are topologically the same. The second claims a pair with multiplicities four and five in four complex variables. Three variables are not covered.
doesNot: This does not settle Zariski’s question in three complex variables, and it does not address families of germs.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: O. Zariski, who posed the multiplicity question
scorecard.significanceWhy: If correct, it answers a well-known 1971 question negatively, down to four variables.

explanation:
Take the polynomial h = T(X − T²)(X − 2T²) in two variables. Multiply it out and you get TX² − 3XT³ + 2T⁵. The terms have total degrees 3, 4 and 5. The lowest is 3, so the multiplicity of h at the origin is 3. The multiplicity is the least total degree of a term that actually appears. It counts how many sheets of the shape h = 0 meet at the origin. Here the three factors give three smooth sheets. The second paper starts its construction from exactly this curve[2].

Now look at the same shape with topology instead. A homeomorphism is a continuous deformation with a continuous inverse. It may stretch and bend, but it may not tear. A germ is a shape seen only near the origin. Two germs are ambiently homeomorphic when a deformation of the surrounding space carries one onto the other. Zariski asked in 1971 whether this embedded topology always determines the multiplicity[1].

For curves in the plane, the answer is yes[3]. In every dimension, a germ that is ambiently homeomorphic to a smooth one is itself smooth. That is the A’Campo–Lê theorem[4]. So multiplicity one can never pair with a larger multiplicity[4]. Many other partial results needed extra assumptions. Some kept a continuous family with a fixed Milnor number, a count of the holes in a nearby smooth slice[5]. Others assumed metric or contact structure, or few variables[6].

The first paper claims a negative answer. It builds two polynomial germs in N complex variables, where N is a multiple of eight and larger than 3[15]. One has multiplicity 2 and the other has multiplicity 3[7]. Both have an isolated critical point at the origin, meaning all partial derivatives vanish together only there[15]. Yet the two zero sets are ambiently homeomorphic[7]. The paper fixes N by exact arithmetic but does not try to make it small[8]. The same pair also answers Arnold’s corank question negatively for ambient topology[9]. The corank is the number of variables minus the rank of the matrix of second derivatives.

The second paper brings the dimension down to four variables. It builds two germs in four complex variables with isolated critical points[10]. One has multiplicity 4 and the other multiplicity 5. Their zero sets are again ambiently homeomorphic[10]. The paper says its argument is independent of the first, with a different dimension and equation format[11]. The case of three variables remains open in both papers[11].

Why was this hard? Topology is usually read from the Milnor fibre, a smooth nearby slice of the shape. Its holes carry an integer pairing called the Seifert form, which records how cycles link. In high dimensions this form decides the embedded topology. Multiplicity, by contrast, is read directly from the lowest-degree terms of an equation[12]. The main difficulty is to keep the two different lowest degrees while making the integer Seifert forms match exactly[13]. Matching rational spectra is not enough. The integer forms must be identified[13].

Families cannot do this. The theorem of Fernández de Bobadilla and Pełka says multiplicity is constant along continuous families with constant Milnor number. So these germs cannot be joined by such a family[14].

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for these papers in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked them. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the proofs hold. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published. The three-variable case remains open.

glossary.meaning: The lowest total degree of a term in the equation of a shape at a point.
A shape considered only in a small neighbourhood of a point.
Related by a continuous, reversible deformation of the surrounding space that carries one shape to the other.
A point where all partial derivatives vanish together, with no other such points nearby.
A smooth nearby slice of a singular shape, used to study its topology.
An integer pairing on the holes of the Milnor fibre that records how cycles link.
The number of variables minus the rank of the matrix of second derivatives at the point.
